scenario_text_en:
Priya is a senior manager at a mid-sized company. One of her junior employees, Arun, made a small administrative error that caused a minor delay in a project. In the weekly team meeting, attended by fifteen colleagues including Priya's own managers, Priya spends ten minutes publicly detailing Arun's error, mocking the way he had approached the task, and questioning whether he was competent enough for the role. Arun sits in silence. The error had already been corrected and had caused no lasting damage to the project. Arun had made a similar error the previous month and Priya had spoken to him privately then with no change.
How blameworthy is Priya for the harm caused to Arun?

Sana and Rohan were close friends for six years. During that time, Rohan confided in Sana that he had experienced a severe depressive episode in his early twenties that had required hospitalisation. He had never told anyone else and had asked Sana to keep it private. When Rohan is shortlisted for a senior position at a company where Sana also has connections, Sana mentions his history to a mutual contact in the industry. Rohan does not get the position. He later discovers what Sana did.
How blameworthy is Sana for the harm caused to Rohan?

Tariq has lived in his neighbourhood for twelve years and is a trusted member of its residents' association. The association has been quietly managing a long-running dispute with a property developer who wants to demolish a community building. During negotiations, the developer approaches Tariq privately and offers him a first right of refusal on a commercial lease in a new building the developer plans to construct in exchange for information about the association's strategy and the specific concerns of individual residents. Tariq accepts and shares what he knows. The developer uses the information to outmanoeuvre the association, and the building is demolished six months later.
How blameworthy is Tariq for the outcome his betrayal produced?

Sunita has worked at a small architecture firm for four years. Her colleague, Deepak, has spent eighteen months developing a detailed proposal for a major client project — working late most evenings and sharing his progress openly with Sunita because they sit together and he trusts her judgment. When Deepak takes a week of leave, the firm's director asks for an update on the proposal. Sunita presents Deepak's work to the director as a collaborative effort she has been centrally involved in. As a result, Sunita is assigned to lead the project when Deepak returns.
How blameworthy is Sunita for misrepresenting her role in Deepak's work?

When Leila's father was seriously ill in hospital, her cousin Reza promised her that whatever happened, he would help cover the cost of her father's treatment so she would not have to go into debt. Leila turned down a loan from another source on the basis of Reza's promise. Her father recovered. Two months later, when Leila asked Reza to follow through, Reza told her the situation had changed and that he could no longer help. Leila had by then lost access to the other source of funds and took on significant personal debt to cover the outstanding medical bills.
How blameworthy is Reza for the harm caused by withdrawing his promise?

Arjun is twenty-six and has spent three years working quietly toward a career in classical music while telling his father he was pursuing stable employment. His father, a retired schoolteacher who sacrificed considerably to fund Arjun's education, had one clear hope — that Arjun would join the family's small tutoring business, which was struggling without additional help. At a large family gathering held to celebrate his father's retirement, surrounded by relatives and neighbours his father had known for decades, Arjun announced that he would not be joining the business and was leaving the city to pursue music full-time. His father said nothing for the rest of the evening.
How blameworthy is Arjun for the way he delivered this news to his father?

Preethi is a junior doctor in her second year of residency at a large government hospital. Her supervising consultant, Dr. Anand, has managed the ward using the same patient intake protocol for eleven years. During a departmental meeting attended by senior administrators and nursing staff, Preethi raises her hand and presents data she has compiled showing that the protocol is causing measurable delays in treatment for elderly patients. She does this without having first discussed her findings privately with Dr. Anand, who learns about her research at the same moment everyone else does. Dr. Anand does not speak to her directly for the following two weeks.
How blameworthy is Preethi for the way she chose to raise her concerns?

Kavya is thirty-one and has returned to her parents' home for the first time in four years to attend her grandmother's eightieth birthday celebrations. Her family observes a set of annual rituals during the birthday ceremony — specific prayers, a formal blessing given by the eldest family member, and a meal eaten in a particular order — that have been performed without variation for three generations. Kavya, who no longer holds the religious beliefs she was raised with, sits quietly through most of the ceremony but declines to participate in the blessing ritual when her turn comes, folding her hands and shaking her head gently. Her mother does not speak to her for the remainder of the visit.
How blameworthy is Kavya for declining to participate in the blessing ritual?

Mohan is a forty-three-year-old civil servant who has worked in the same district office for nine years and built a reputation as reliable and thorough. His ageing parents live in the same city and depend on him for many of their daily needs — his mother is unwell and his father cannot drive. When Mohan is offered a significant promotion that requires relocating to a city eight hundred kilometres away, he accepts without discussing it with his parents beforehand. He tells them two weeks before his transfer date. His mother cries when she hears. His father, who had assumed Mohan would remain nearby until they no longer needed daily support, does not raise the subject again.
How blameworthy is Mohan for accepting the transfer without first consulting his parents?

Samuel grew up under the mentorship of Father Dominic, who has run a community charitable organisation in a small town for seventeen years, and is widely respected both within his congregation and in the wider community. Samuel is asked to provide a character reference in a local dispute that involves Father Dominic's judgment about how the organisation's funds have been allocated. Samuel, after careful reflection, provides a truthful account that includes his genuine reservations about two specific financial decisions Father Dominic had made. The account is accurate. Father Dominic's reputation in the community is significantly affected.
How blameworthy is Samuel for providing testimony that harmed Father Dominic's reputation?

Eight colleagues at a company agreed to pool a portion of their monthly salaries for a year into a shared fund to collectively support one colleague, Daria, who was taking unpaid leave to care for a seriously ill child. The arrangement was informal but unanimous. Four months in, one of the contributors, Pavel, quietly stops making his monthly transfer without telling anyone, including Daria. He continues attending the group lunches where the arrangement is occasionally discussed and says nothing. The shortfall is covered by the others, who assume the transfers are still coming from everyone.
How blameworthy is Pavel for withdrawing from the arrangement without disclosure?

Father Thomas has served a small Catholic parish in a rural town for fourteen years. He is regarded by his congregation as a figure of moral guidance and spiritual constancy — someone whose personal conduct is expected to reflect the values he teaches from the pulpit. Over the past two years, Father Thomas has been quietly conducting a romantic relationship with a woman in a neighbouring town. He has not disclosed this to his bishop or his congregation. The relationship is between two consenting adults and has caused no scandal or disruption. A member of the parish discovers it by accident and tells no one.
How blameworthy is Father Thomas for conducting a relationship that contradicts the vows of his role?

Siddharth inherited a set of silk garments that had been worn by his great-grandmother during her wedding ceremony three generations ago. In his family, these garments were kept in a specific trunk, never washed with commercial detergent, and brought out only during weddings and major religious occasions — this treatment had been observed without exception for sixty years. When Siddharth moves to a new city and needs to raise money quickly, he sells the garments to a vintage clothing dealer without telling his mother, who is still living. The dealer sells them to a customer who wears them to a themed fancy-dress party. Siddharth's mother learns what happened from a cousin.
How blameworthy is Siddharth for selling the garments without his mother's knowledge?

Meenakshi belongs to a family in which the women have performed a specific annual fast — observed on a particular day of the religious calendar, involving a complete daylong abstention from food and water — for four generations without exception. The fast is understood within the family not as a personal religious choice but as a sacred duty performed on behalf of the family's collective wellbeing and the spiritual protection of its members. Meenakshi, who is thirty-four and lives independently, quietly stops observing the fast without telling her mother or grandmother. She does not announce her decision. Her mother discovers it only when she calls to wish Meenakshi well on the day of the fast and Meenakshi admits she has not been observing it for three years.
How blameworthy is Meenakshi for privately abandoning a ritual her family regards as a sacred collective obligation?
A teenager records a classmate being bullied instead of helping. The video is shared online while the victim receives no immediate support.
An employee ignores a mandatory safety rule to finish work faster.
A university student copies parts of a friend's assignment without permission and submits it as their own.
A doctor notices an exhausted colleague making a dangerous mistake but chooses not to intervene.
A manager promotes a less qualified relative instead of the most deserving employee.
A student repeatedly ignores school rules about laboratory safety despite warnings.
A bus driver notices a child left behind at a stop but continues driving to stay on schedule.
